sections.text: Here are heroes, mighty archers, equal in battle to Bhima and Arjuna, Yoyudhana (Satyaki), Virata and Drupada, of the great car (mighty warriors).
Dhrishtaketu, chekitana and the valiant king of Kasi, Purujit and Kuntibhoja and Saibya, the best men.
The strong Yodhamanyu and the brave Uttamaujas, the son of Subhadra (Abhimanyu, the son of Subhadra and Arjuna), and the sons of Draupadi, all of great chariots (great heroes).

Well be discussing Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 1, Arjuna Vishada Yoga, the Yoga of Arjunas Grief. In our scriptural system, there are two types of scripture, divided into two major categories. One is called Shruti. The other is called Smriti.
Shruti means heard and Smriti means remembered. The scriptures considered heard by the great sages in their contemplation, in their inspired moments, and then given out to the world, are considered Shrutis. Based on those scriptures, the truths found in Shruti, the systems, laws, customs, and traditions of society were developed; these are called Smritis. Shrutis are typically considered as Prasthana Trayi. There are three legs of Shruti. One is the Upanishads, which we have all learned.
They come at the end of the Vedas. Vedas generally describe all types of sciences which are utilitarian or material in nature, things one can use in his lifetime. But at the end of the Vedas, there are dialogues between students and teachers. They are called Upanishads. They deal with the fundamental questions we all ask, knowingly or unknowingly: Who am I? Is there someone who has control over my life, and what is my relationship with that controller?
So these are dialogues between students and teachers, set in the serene environment of Himalayan valleys. Both students and teachers are highly evolved seekers. The teacher is a realized master who has gone through his Sadhana and realized the truth. The student is also a highly evolved seeker who has gone through Sadhana and is now finding his final answers.
The truths in Srutis are immutable. Rather, they cannot be changed over a period of time, from one age to another. The Shruti does not change. The truths revealed in Srutis do not change. Smriti, on the other hand, are the laws created by society, by the leaders of the society. The lawmakers in the society are adaptable to the new environment in the society.
So the two mains we hear about are Parasara and Manusmriti. Mainly manusmriti is the one which we hear most, we heard most about. In fact, if Im not mistaken, the laws in India before independence and somewhat after the independence were structured based on Manusmriti. Laws for Hindus were Hindu laws and they were based on Manusmriti. And laws for Muslims were based on Syria. So the Manusmriti was considered the code of conduct for the society.
As we know, we dont apply Manusmriti as-is in our society now. Even in India, the laws have changed, society has changed. The basic structure may remain what Manusmriti says, but many things we have updated to fit our current needs. On the other hand, the facts revealed in Shruti are unchangeable. It is something like mathematics, I can use mathematics in my life from childhood to old age, depending on my own needs, and Ill interpret mathematics accordingly.
But the fundamentals of mathematics do not change. 2+2 remained 4 when I was in kindergarten; it still remains 4 when Im an old man and consider myself a wise person. The spiritual tenets in Shruti are like those rules, unchangeable. They remain constant no matter how you look at it or try to prove it. But the application of those laws can change according to society. The way I used mathematics in my childhood is different from how I used it as a high school student, then as a college student, and then as a professional.
My applications are different based on my own situation. So Smritis are like those adaptable sciences which we can update as we go along in our society. The fundamentals of Manusmriti may remain the same, but the application is completely changed in our society now. So there are three aspects of the Shruti: the Upanishads as we talked about, Brahma Sutra, and third is Bhagavad Gita. Bhagavad Gita is considered an Upanishad by itself.
Therefore, at the end of every chapter we say Upanishadsu Bhagavad Gita. Its considered an Upanishad by itself because it reveals the truths found in Shruti. But the uniqueness of Bhagavad Gita is that it is also considered Smriti, its a combination of Shruti and Smriti. Therefore it has a unique place in Prasthana Trayi.
In Prasthana Trayi, if you just learn Upanishads, they are transcendental. They transcend my day-to-day life, telling me what the ultimate truth is and how it relates to me. And they are set in a very serene environment, as I said before. Bhagavad Gita, on the other hand, is set in a completely different environment. Its still a dialogue between a student and a teacher.
But here the student and teacher are not a great master and a lowly seeker trying to understand. They were two friends, a dialogue between two friends, two cousins. One was great, but he did not act like one when it comes to his friendship. So its a dialogue between two equals, set in an environment completely different from Himalayan valleys, its on the battlefield. Some commentators think that the whole Mahabharata was written by Bhagavan Ved Vyas.
To have a platform for Bhagavad Gita, he had to have a proper background to convert it into a scripture that can guide mankind. The entire Mahabharata, which is a hundred thousand verses as we now know it, originally started out as a book called Jaya with only 24,000 verses. But it did have Bhagavad Gita in it. Bhagavad Gita is the central crown jewel of Mahabharata. Mahabharata became the greatest epic of all times for Hindu culture, for India, and for the world because of Bhagavad Gita. Remove Bhagavad Gita and Mahabharata becomes another story of a Kuru clan.
At the same token, remove Mahabharata and Bhagavad Gita becomes merely poetry, something similar to Upanishads. They have a symbiotic relationship. Mahabharata converts Bhagavad Gita into a Smriti which can be used in day-to-day life. Mahabharata gives us the background of human society, human conditions, human aspirations, human shortcomings. It is generally said that Mahabharata contains all human situations. If you dont find a situation in Mahabharata, it does not exist.
You may find any situation from Mahabharata in other works of art, but not the other way around. So Mahabharata sets the stage, and we all know the story, the cousins Kauravas and Pandavas were fighting for their rights, and Duryodhana said hes not giving even a square inch of land, even though rightfully Pandavas were the claimants for that kingdom. The war is about to begin, and we are now going to see a dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna.
In the first chapter, called Arjuna Vishada Yoga, there are no great philosophical revelations, so one should not seek philosophical explanations in Chapter 1. Bhagavan Shankaracharya in his Gita Bhashya does not start his commentary until verse 11 of Chapter 2. He didnt think it was worth his time to talk about Chapter 1 and the first 10 verses of Chapter 2.
But for us common folks, context is very important. Without context, we lose the meaning of what we are discussing. Chapter 1 gives us the context for the dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna.
Krishna and Arjuna are the two main characters in this dialogue, but there are two other people involved in Bhagavad Gita: Dhritarashtra and Sanjaya. Dhritarashtra, as we know, was the King of Hastinapur. Duryodhana and the other Kauravas were his sons, and he could have avoided this war by just his own declaration, but he did not. He was blind from birth and therefore was not considered worthy of being king. But because of the situation with Pandu, the younger son, he was made the caretaker king, and Duryodhana became the effective king, like MBS in Saudi Arabia.
Duryodhana was the one actually making the decisions, and he obviously was not going to give up the kingdom he had already been enjoying for so many years. When the war is about to begin, Dhritarashtra is still sitting in the palace because hes not taking part in the war, but hes curious about whats going on. He knew that the Kaurava side has 11 Akshauhini Sena and the Pandavas have 7, so 11 plus 7 is 18. You will see that 18 is the magic number: there are 18 books in Mahabharata, the war lasted 18 days, and there are 18 chapters in Bhagavad Gita.
Apparently one Akshauhini has 21,870 chariots, the same number of elephants, three times that of horses, and five times that of foot soldiers. If you take any of these numbers and add their digits, they will add up to 18. Take 21,870 and add up the digits, it adds up to 18. Multiply that by three, and the digits add up to 18 again. Multiply by five, same result.
If you do the math, there were about 4 million people on that battlefield. Now, Ive never been to Kurukshetra, so I cant tell you its large enough to hold 4 million people. But according to this calculation, about 4 million soldiers were ready to fight. The war is about to begin. Dhritarashtra knew that his side is much stronger, 11 Akshauhini versus Pandavas 7.
But he also knew who is on the right side and who was on the wrong side. That gives you a little pause in thinking about what is going to happen. He wanted to know whats going on, and he had an opportunity. The day before, Bhagavan Vyasa stopped by his palace and said, You really need to see whats happening, and I can give you divine vision so that you can see it. But he said, Im comfortable in my blindness. I really dont want to see.
But if you are really kind enough, give it to my minister Sanjaya. So Sanjaya got the Divya Drishti, the divine vision. Now, we do not know how all that happened. Maybe Sanjaya was on the battlefield and reported back. But it is believed that Sanjaya had this divine vision, not only could he see things happening on the battlefield, but he could also see whats going on in peoples minds. He can hear, he can see, and he can perceive.
Therefore its called Divya Drishti, he has much greater capacity than an average person. Ati Drishti means he can see even further than a normal person. Dhritarashtra knew that Sanjaya can see everything. So the very first verse starts with Dhritarashtra Uvacha. Notice that Bhagavad Gita did not start with Krishna Uvacha or Bhagavan Uvacha or Arjuna Uvacha. It started with Dhritarashtra, the blind king. These characters are there in Chapter 1 and in Mahabharata.
So we can identify with the situation. I may not be able to identify with Arjuna, but I can probably identify with Dhritarashtra as a father. Maybe I have done something that Dhritarashtra did, and therefore suffered.

These verses enumerate the mighty Pandava warriors: Yuyudhana (Satyaki), Virata, Drupada, Dhrishtaketu, Chekitana, the King of Kashi, Purujit, Kuntibhoja, Shaibya, Yudhamanyu, Uttamaujas, Abhimanyu, and the sons of Draupadi, all described as maharathas (great chariot warriors). Notice that Duryodhana is reciting this list not to his commander Bhishma, but to his teacher Drona. This reveals his anxiety: hes essentially saying, Look at all these students you trained who are now fighting against us. When we feel insecure about our position, we often seek validation from those we hope to influence.
Reflect on times when youve enumerated your competitors strengths to someone whose loyalty you questioned. Perhaps before a presentation, you listed all the reasons the other team might win, hoping for reassurance. This is the Duryodhana pattern, anxiety masquerading as assessment. The Gita shows us that true security doesnt come from counting resources or comparing strengths, but from alignment with dharma.
Consider also the teaching embedded in Bhagavad Gitas structure: it is both Shruti (revealed scripture revealing eternal truths) and Smriti (remembered wisdom applicable to daily life). Unlike the Upanishads set in serene Himalayan valleys, this dialogue unfolds on a battlefield between two friends and cousins. What battles are you facing right now in your workplace, family, or inner life? The Gita meets us not in some ideal spiritual environment, but precisely where we are, in the midst of our conflicts, confusions, and competing loyalties. How might you bring the wisdom of scripture to your own Kurukshetra today?
